name: Senegal
summary: Independent from France in 1960 under the poet-president Léopold Senghor; one of Africa’s most stable democracies, never having had a coup.

knownFor.label: Gorée Island
knownFor.note: Memorial to the Atlantic slave trade.

knownFor.label: Thieboudienne
knownFor.note: Fish and rice, the national dish.

location.value: The westernmost point of mainland Africa; 196,722 km².

terrain.value: Low plains and the Senegal River valley.

climate.value: A Sahel climate with a short rainy season, drier in the north and wetter in the south.

resources.value: Fish, groundnuts, phosphates; oil and gas since 2024.

disasters.value: Droughts in the 1970s–80s and floods in the Dakar suburbs.

urbanisation.value: Dakar, on the Cap-Vert peninsula, is the largest city, followed by Touba, a holy city of the Mouride order.

disease.value: Malaria, with cases falling after bed-net and treatment campaigns.

migration.value: Emigration to Europe, sometimes by dangerous boat journeys.

economicBase.value: Fishing is the main foreign-exchange earner (3.2% of GDP, about 600,000 jobs); groundnuts are a primary crop and phosphates a historic export; oil and gas are now being exploited. The page gives no production figures.

tradeRoutes.value: The port of Dakar serves Senegal and landlocked Mali.

wealth.value: A lower-middle-income country, with oil and gas starting in 2024.

moneyAndTax.value: The West African CFA franc, shared with neighbours and pegged to the euro.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A unitary semi-presidential republic with a 150-seat National Assembly.

keyRulers.value: Léopold Sédar Senghor (president 1960–80). Later and present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: Peaceful elections; never a successful coup.

stability.value: Stable; separatist conflict in Casamance since 1982, with talks with rebels in Rome in December 2012.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: A professional army that has stayed out of politics.

majorWars.value: Clashes between government forces and the separatist MFDC in Casamance since 1982; the page says the conflict had not been fully concluded as of 2025.

territoryChange.value: Part of the Mali Federation with French Sudan until 20 August 1960.

alliancesRivals.value: Close to France and a member of ECOWAS; it has helped mediate regional conflicts.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Cheikh Anta Diop University in Dakar, one of the oldest in West Africa (1957).

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Roads; a new train to the airport (2021).

religion.value: Sources differ: the infobox gives 91% Muslim and 5% Christian, Pew 89.0% Muslim and 10.0% Christian, and the CIA 97.2% Muslim. The Sufi brotherhoods are not covered in the part of the page read.

languageWriting.value: French is official; Wolof is the most widely spoken language, with Pulaar, Serer and others.

socialStructure.value: Wolof, Fula, Serer and other peoples; traditional castes.

sharedIdentity.value: The concept of “teranga” (hospitality) is a point of national pride.

dailyLife.value: Many families eat thieboudienne (rice and fish) and drink attaya tea.

neighbours.value: Mauritania, Mali, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, The Gambia.

ideasReligions.value: Négritude, the movement of Black pride led by Léopold Senghor, and Sufi Islamic brotherhoods.

colonisation.value: A French colony (part of French West Africa) until 1960.

riseSignals.value: Independence on 20 June 1960 as part of the Mali Federation, which broke up on 20 August 1960.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Senegal continues as an independent republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
